text: Mercury circles the Sun every 88 Earth days, faster than any other planet.
Mercury has no air to hold heat, so nights can drop to about -290 F.
Mercury is a little more than one third the width of Earth.
Sunlight takes about 3.2 minutes to reach Mercury.
Venus is the hottest planet, about 872 F at the surface, hot enough to melt lead.
The air pressure at the surface of Venus is about 93 times that at Earth's sea level.
Winds at the tops of Venus's clouds have been measured as high as 224 mph.
Venus takes 584 days to go through all its phases, while our Moon takes about a month.
Earth takes 365.25 days to go once around the Sun, so calendars need leap years.
Earth's axis is tilted 23.4 degrees from its orbit plane, which gives us seasons.
Earth's oceans gave life a place to begin about 3.8 billion years ago.
One rotation of Earth takes 23.9 hours, a little less than 24.
Mars is about half the size of Earth.
check: about half the size of Earth

text: A Martian day is called a sol and lasts 24.6 hours.
A year on Mars lasts 669.6 sols, the same as 687 Earth days.
Sunlight needs about 13 minutes to reach Mars.
If Jupiter were a hollow shell, 1,000 Earths could fit inside it.
Jupiter has the shortest day in the solar system, about 9.9 hours.
One year on Jupiter is about 12 Earth years.
A day on Saturn lasts only 10.7 hours.
Saturn's main rings span up to 175,000 miles but are typically only about 30 feet thick.
Saturn takes about 29.4 Earth years to orbit the Sun once.
The Cassini Division, a gap 2,920 miles wide, separates Saturn's A and B rings.
Uranus spins nearly sideways, at about a 90-degree angle to its orbit.
William Herschel found Uranus in 1781 and first thought it was a comet or a star.
One year on Uranus is about 84 Earth years.
Neptune finished its first orbit since its discovery in 2011, after 165 years.
Neptune was the first planet found by mathematical prediction, not by looking.
Sunlight takes about 4 hours to reach Neptune, and Earth's daylight is about 900 times brighter.
Apollo astronauts brought back 842 pounds of lunar rocks and soil.
More than 105 robotic spacecraft have been launched to explore the Moon.
Humans first saw the far side of the Moon in 1959, from a Soviet spacecraft.
The Moon is on average 238,855 miles from Earth.
The Moon takes about 27.3 days to orbit Earth.
New moon to new moon takes about 29.5 days.
The Sun is about 100 times wider than Earth.
The Sun's core is about 27 million F, hot enough for nuclear fusion.
The Sun spins once in 25 Earth days at its equator but 36 days at its poles.
The Sun formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a disk of gas and dust.
The International Space Station circles Earth about every 90 minutes.
The space station makes 16 orbits a day, so its crew sees 16 sunrises and sunsets.
People have lived aboard the space station continuously since November 2000.
The station's solar array wingspan, 356 feet, beats an Airbus A380's 262 feet.
GPS is a system of more than 30 navigation satellites circling Earth.
The first satellite picture of Earth was taken by Explorer 6 on August 14, 1959.
TIROS-1 sent the first TV picture of Earth from space in 1960.
NASA's Aqua satellite launched May 4, 2002 with six Earth-observing instruments.
CloudSat was planned for 22 months of cloud radar but worked for over 17 years.
CloudSat carried a 94-GHz radar to see the vertical structure of clouds from space.
Landsat satellites have imaged Earth's land since 1972.
Landsat's free data added an estimated $25.6 billion to the US economy in 2023.
Landsat's archive shows how cities grew, coasts shifted, and forests changed since the 1970s.
About 30 percent of incoming sunlight is reflected back to space.
A cumulonimbus cloud can have a top reaching about 10 km (33,000 feet) or more.
Satellites only detect about 25 percent of fires burning worldwide, but those are the largest ones.
In 1998, smoke from fires in southern Mexico cut visibility to 2 km in parts of Texas.
About 90 percent of aerosols, by mass, come from natural sources.
Dust from North Africa can spread across the Atlantic Ocean, as seen in satellite imagery.
Without the greenhouse effect, Earth's average surface would be about 0 F, not 59 F.
Roughly 30 percent of sunlight is reflected into space by clouds and ice.
Carbon dioxide levels rose nearly 38 percent between about 1750 and 2009.
Most ozone sits in the stratosphere, 10 to 40 km up, shielding us from ultraviolet rays.
An ozone molecule is made of three oxygen atoms.
The ocean's biological carbon pump moves about 10 gigatonnes of carbon to the deep sea yearly.
Global sea level rose between 10 and 25 cm during the 20th century.
Coastal populations were about 23 percent of the world's people in 1990.
Volcanic sulfate aerosols from Pinatubo in 1991 warmed the tropical stratosphere by 4 kelvin.
About 96.5 percent of Earth's water is in the global oceans.
Only a thousandth of one percent of Earth's water is water vapor in the air.
Earth holds about 1.39 billion cubic kilometers of water.
Evaporation from oceans and lakes supplies nearly 90 percent of the moisture in our air.
In the last 800,000 years there have been eight cycles of ice ages and warm periods.
The last ice age ended about 11,700 years ago.
Scientists showed the heat-trapping nature of carbon dioxide in the mid-19th century.
Titan is nearly 50 percent wider than Earth's Moon.
Christiaan Huygens discovered Saturn's moon Titan on March 25, 1655.
Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.

text: Pluto is about 3.6 billion miles from the Sun.
Giuseppe Piazzi spotted Ceres, the first asteroid belt object found, in 1801.
When Dawn arrived in 2015, Ceres became the first dwarf planet visited by a spacecraft.
check: first dwarf planet to receive a visit

text: Comets are leftovers from the birth of the solar system about 4.6 billion years ago.
Vesta, the largest asteroid, is about 329 miles across.
More than 150 asteroids are known to have small companion moons.
The nearest known black hole, Gaia BH1, is about 1,500 light-years away.
The most massive black hole observed, TON 618, weighs 66 billion times the Sun.
Stars orbiting near the Milky Way's center proved it holds a supermassive black hole.
Hubble was launched on April 24, 1990.
Webb orbits the Sun 1.5 million kilometers from Earth, at a point called L2.
Webb has a 5-layer sunshield to block infrared from the Sun, Earth, and Moon.
Webb can see back over 13.5 billion years to the first galaxies after the Big Bang.
Hubble orbits 560 kilometers above Earth.
Parker Solar Probe will come within about 3.9 million miles of the Sun.
Parker Solar Probe was planned to make 24 orbits of the Sun over seven years.
Juno's first orbit of Jupiter stretched across 53 days.
Saturn was Cassini's home for 13 years.
New Horizons reached the Kuiper belt object Arrokoth in 2019.
New Horizons was the first spacecraft to explore Pluto up close, on July 14, 2015.
Perseverance passed Opportunity's Mars driving record of 28.06 miles.
Perseverance launched on July 30, 2020 to look for signs of ancient microbial life on Mars.
Curiosity climbed 1 kilometer in elevation up Mount Sharp, starting from Gale Crater.
Ingenuity was meant for five test flights but completed 72 flights over nearly three years.
On April 19, 2021 Ingenuity flew the first powered, controlled flight on Mars.
The Kepler space telescope launched on March 6, 2009.
Kepler's telescope had a 1-meter aperture and the largest digital camera sent to space then.
TESS has found nearly 6,000 confirmed or candidate exoplanets as of September 2025.
DART hit Dimorphos, a moonlet just 530 feet across, on September 26, 2022.
Dimorphos orbits a larger asteroid called Didymos, which is 2,560 feet across.
OSIRIS-REx collected rocks and dust from asteroid Bennu on October 20, 2020.
Europa Clipper is traveling 1.8 billion miles to reach Jupiter in April 2030.
Apollo 11 launched on July 16, 1969, carrying Armstrong, Aldrin, and Collins.
The Oort Cloud lies between 5,000 and 100,000 astronomical units from the Sun.
At a million miles a day, Voyager 1 will not reach the Oort Cloud for about 300 years.
The Perseid meteors are pieces of comet Swift-Tuttle, which swings by the Sun every 135 years.
Our solar system takes about 230 million years to orbit the center of the galaxy.
The solar system moves around the galaxy at about 515,000 mph.
Voyager 1 crossed into interstellar space in August 2012.
Voyager 2 is the only spacecraft to visit Uranus and Neptune.
check: only spacecraft to visit Uranus and Neptune

text: Sunspot numbers rise and fall in a natural 11-year cycle.
Sunspots typically stretch 1,000 to 100,000 miles across.
One high tide to the next takes a little over 12 hours.
